query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding alloying elements that enhance phase stability and dislocation movement to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys in their initial, unalloyed state
generation.intervention: Adding alloying elements such as Ti, Zr, Hf, V, and Ta to the refractory high-entropy alloys
generation.mechanism: The added alloying elements will enhance phase stability and dislocation movement, leading to improved mechanical performance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical performance, including increased strength and ductility, while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability
generation.baseline: The mechanical performance of refractory high-entropy alloys without the added alloying elements
generation.boundary: The optimal composition and concentration of the added alloying elements, beyond which the benefits may diminish or adverse effects may occur
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal composition and concentration of the added alloying elements, as well as the potential interactions between the alloying elements and the refractory high-entropy alloy matrix

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare refractory high-entropy alloy samples with and without the added alloying elements, and subject them to high-temperature and irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the added alloying elements do not improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability, the hypothesis is falsified

In the process of pursuing high-performance materials, the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [] were introduced. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,]. Research about the effect of alloying elements on the performance of HEAs has predominantly concentrated on the mechanical properties while the literature indicates that conventional and high-entropy alloys and Y and Hf co-doping can effectively enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance of alloys [,,]. Contrary to conventional alloys, which consist of alloying element(s) added to one or two principal elements, HEAs contain five to thirteen equimolar or near-equimolar principal elements between 5 to 35 at.%; hence, the term “multi-principal component alloy” (MCA) is sometimes used. Single-phase HEA is expected to form frequently due to its high mixing entropy, but the microstructure of some HEAs typically shows two or more phases. Moreover, in contrast to the intermetallic structure commonly found in conventional alloys, HEAs exhibit simple BCC, FCC, HCP or a mixture of these crystal structures due to their good mutual solubility, , such as WNbMoTa and WNbMoTaV, , which show a single-phase BCC crystal structure. The purpose of incorporating multiple principal elements is to produce a high-entropy solid solution with improved engineering characteristics, . The excellent properties of HEAs, including their enhanced mechanical strength even at high temperatures along with improved wear and oxidation resistance, fatigue and high-temperature fracture resistance, good thermal stability and toughness, , , , , ,  reflect their potential for use in aerospace, nuclear, ,  and other industri

Granberg et al. () combined experiments and modeling to identify the sluggish mobility of dislocation loops as the main mechanism leading to radiation tolerance in Ni-based FCC HEAs. Kumar et al. () showed how Ni-based FCC HEAs lead to less radiation-induced segregation and fewer voids, although hardness was observed to increase after irradiation. Other studies show results in the same direction, with HEAs improving radiation tolerance in both FCC and BCC structures (). Very recently, W-based quinary HEAs with diverse composition have been synthesized as potential materials for fusion applications. The authors observed the formation of Ti carbides and laves phases at large W concentrations. The authors studied the mechanical response, showing that these materials could lead to twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening (). However, refractory HEAs have never been tested under irradiation for potential uses as PFMs or structural materials in nuclear fusion environments.
